r: Integrated Biology and Earth Science builds gen-ed scientific literacy for future elementary teacher candidates: the building blocks of life, evolution, ecosystem structure, terrestrial and atmospheric processes, and the solar system, taught through lecture plus hands-on laboratory experiments. The applied task is synthesizing and explaining foundational scientific content, an activity language models already perform fluently for textbook-level material, giving real near-term exposure to the explanatory work. Task-exposure research nonetheless classifies science and critical-thinking skills as strongly negatively associated with exposure relative to writing tasks, and the laboratory component adds a hands-on, equipment-based dimension that resists full digitization. The binding constraint at 24 months is the GT-SC1 statewide transfer designation, a course-carrying general-education mandate that requires the course to exist regardless of AI capability. Instrumental need is intact; students still complete labs and learn content themselves.

By 2031, AI tutoring and explanation tools will be materially better at walking students through biology and earth-science concepts, and observed-usage data already shows science-adjacent explanatory tasks well represented in consumer use, pushing conceptual delivery toward augmentation or partial substitution. But the course pairs content with physical laboratory investigation — collecting and interpreting real specimens, materials, and instruments — which task-exposure frameworks keep in a lower-exposure band than pure explanation. The GT-Pathways transfer mandate does not restructure within a catalog cycle, so the course's existence and general-studies function persist regardless of how much explanatory content AI can generate. The instrumental case erodes somewhat as students could self-serve some content, but the lab and the transfer requirement keep the rating from advancing past Medium.

A decade of capability growth plausibly makes AI a highly competent explainer and even a lab-prep assistant for introductory biology and earth science, meaningfully eroding the case that a student needs formal instruction purely to acquire declarative content. Central-case diffusion trends suggest such tools become common in gen-ed classrooms well before 2036, though adoption still lags capability considerably, per Census BTOS-documented diffusion rates well below the technology's demonstrated capability. What is not eroded in the central case is the GT-SC1 transfer mandate, a statutory-adjacent gen-ed requirement immune to AI progress, and the embodied laboratory work — collecting samples, running instruments, recording observations — which keeps a meaningful non-digital core. The honest uncertainty is how much lecture content shrinks around a persistent lab-and-transfer core; the rating holds at Medium rather than climbing to High.
SCI 2600.d: In this course, students examine the application of fundamental scientific principles in biology and earth systems by examining the basic building blocks of life, evolution of life, the human body, ecosystem structure and development, terrestrial formations and surface processes, atmospheric processes, the solar system, and the universe. This class includes laboratory experiments, with a focus on biology and earth science.

r: Integrated Physics and Chemistry covers energy, matter, and their interactions through lecture and hands-on laboratory experiments in basic physics and chemistry, serving elementary teacher candidates' general-education science requirement. The applied task is again conceptual synthesis and explanation of foundational physical-science principles, work that AI performs competently for standard textbook material, and quantitative problem-solving in physics is among the more AI-tractable content types. Task-exposure research still places science and critical-thinking skill strongly on the low-exposure side relative to writing-heavy work, and physical laboratory manipulation of instruments and reagents adds an embodied dimension current models cannot perform. The binding constraint is the GT-SC1 designation, a hard transfer mandate independent of instructional method. At 24 months the course remains fully required; explanatory exposure has not translated into removed instrumental need.

By 2031, AI explanation and problem-solving tools for introductory physics and chemistry will be considerably stronger, and given the capability-growth trend documented by METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months, quantitative science tutoring is a plausible near-term augmentation target that could handle much routine problem-set work. That raises exposure on the conceptual-delivery side of the course. The countervailing forces are unchanged: the laboratory component requires physically manipulating apparatus, reagents, and instruments, an embodied task category that stays protected, and the GT-Pathways general-studies designation locks the course into the transfer core across catalog cycles regardless of how AI-capable the explanatory content becomes. The instrumental case softens compared to 24 months but does not collapse, landing at Medium as the transfer mandate and lab work continue to require the course's existence.

Over a decade, AI capability applied to physics and chemistry problem sets and conceptual explanation will likely be strong enough that a student could learn much of the declarative content independently, and broader classroom AI diffusion by the mid-2030s is plausible under a central-case adoption trajectory, though Census BTOS-documented diffusion still lags capability considerably. Still unresolved by pure capability gains is the GT-SC1 transfer requirement, which persists as an institutional fact regardless of pedagogy, and the hands-on laboratory investigations that give the course a physical, instrument-based core. The genuine uncertainty is whether lecture delivery is restructured around AI tutoring while labs persist largely unchanged; the rating holds at Medium, protected by transfer mandate and embodiment rather than by low task exposure alone.
SCI 2610.d: In this course, students examine the nature of energy and matter, their interactions and changes, and the application of fundamental scientific concepts to the study of our natural world. Students explore these concepts through hands-on laboratory experiments that focus on basic physics and chemistry principles.

r: Secondary Science Methods trains teacher candidates in choosing, developing, and implementing science curriculum, aligning instruction to state and national standards, designing inclusive and anti-racist assessment, coordinating family engagement, and managing laboratory safety. Curriculum drafting and standards-alignment documentation are increasingly assisted by AI lesson-planning tools already circulating among practicing teachers, giving real exposure to that administrative slice of the work. But the course's core competence — pedagogical judgment about how students learn science, live safety supervision, and equity-minded assessment design for real classrooms — sits in low-exposure, high-presence categories, and errors in inclusive assessment or lab safety carry real cost, keeping verification burden meaningful. No general-studies designation caps this upper-division course, but its role inside the CO teacher-licensure sequence functions as a strong program mandate. Instrumental need is intact at 24 months.

By 2031, AI-assisted lesson planning, standards alignment, and assessment drafting will be commonplace in teacher-preparation coursework, and productivity research on professional-writing tasks suggests real time savings on these documentation-heavy activities, further easing the verification burden as candidates learn to review AI-generated materials rather than build everything from scratch. That shifts the administrative portion of the course toward augmentation. The pedagogical core — translating child-development and science-learning theory into live, safety-conscious, equity-minded instruction — remains resistant, since it is judgment-laden and interpersonally embodied. The course's position inside Colorado's licensure-tied secondary science preparation sequence continues to function as a program-level mandate that does not loosen within a catalog cycle. The instrumental case softens on the documentation side; the rating advances to Medium, not higher.

A decade of sustained capability growth could make AI a genuinely strong co-planner for science curriculum and assessment design, and if diffusion into teacher-preparation programs keeps pace with capability, the administrative core of this course could shrink substantially by the mid-2030s. What is unlikely to shrink in the central case is Colorado's licensure-linked requirement that candidates complete this specific methods sequence as an approved component of the preparation program, and the live pedagogical judgment — managing lab safety, differentiating instruction for diverse learners, engaging families — that no automated tool performs on the candidate's behalf. The uncertainty band is wide regarding how much curriculum work becomes AI-drafted-then-reviewed versus AI-independent. The rating holds at Medium, reflecting real erosion in documentation tasks offset by the licensure-tied program mandate and enduring in-person pedagogical core.
SCI 3950.d: Secondary Science Methods explores the nature of science and inquiry in preparation for teaching science in a secondary school environment. Teacher candidates learn to choose, develop, and implement curriculum based upon students' needs, a deep understanding of how people learn science, and how to align with both state and national content standards. Inclusive and anti- racist approaches to student assessment, family engagement, safety, and professional development are also emphasized.

r: This is a 60-hour supervised field placement in a secondary science classroom: teacher candidates design and implement lessons, prepare and supervise laboratory investigations, and adjust instruction for students with diverse needs, under direct classroom-teacher and Office of Clinical Experiences supervision. The applied work is in-person instructional delivery, real-time lab safety supervision, and adaptive teaching with actual adolescents — precisely the embodied, high-presence categories task-exposure research places at the low end of automation exposure. The binding constraint is a hard, course-specific institutional lock: Colorado educator licensure requires logged, supervised clinical field hours that an AI system cannot satisfy, and this placement is arranged directly by the university's clinical-experiences office. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised, embodied field practice is completely untouched by AI capability.

By 2031, AI tools will likely assist practicing science teachers with lesson drafting, differentiation suggestions, and lab-safety checklists, and candidates in this placement may well use such tools while planning their lessons. That augments preparation but does not substitute for the field hours themselves: the course exists to certify supervised, real-time performance in front of live adolescent students, handling actual laboratory hazards and unpredictable classroom dynamics. Verification burden is real because safety and equity failures with minors carry high cost and are not always obvious in the moment, keeping a present, trained human supervisor necessary. Colorado's field-hour licensure requirement does not relax within a catalog cycle or two. The rating stays Low; AI reshapes what candidates plan, not whether they must physically be in the room.

Even under a decade of aggressive capability growth and broad classroom-AI diffusion, the requirement that a secondary science teacher candidate accumulate supervised, in-person clinical field hours — physically managing lab safety and instruction with real adolescent students — is among the most durable constraints in the catalog, with no credible central-case path to its removal via licensure reform by 2036. The embodied, real-time, safety-critical nature of the work resists substitution categorically, not incrementally, regardless of how capable planning or tutoring tools become. Genuine uncertainty exists about how heavily AI mediates the lesson content candidates deliver during these hours, but not about whether the supervised field placement itself remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the clinical clock-hour licensure mandate.
SCI 3960.d: This 60-hour field experience provides opportunities to develop teacher candidates' professional and pedagogical skills in a science classroom. In coordination with the classroom teacher, teacher candidates design and implement science content lessons, prepare for and supervise laboratory investigations, and adjust science instruction for students with diverse needs. Course assignments and evaluations are designed to help teacher candidates become reflective practitioners. Field placements are arranged by the Office of Clinical Experiences & Partnerships in collaboration with local schools. Social Work
